what_its_for: Bisacodyl is a laxative used to treat occasional constipation or to empty your bowels before a medical procedure or surgery. It works by stimulating your intestines to move stool through your body more quickly.
how_to_take: Bisacodyl comes as a tablet you swallow and as a suppository you place into your rectum. For tablets: swallow them whole with a full glass of water — do not crush, chew, or break them. Do not take tablets within 1 hour of drinking milk or taking antacids or dairy products, as this can cause stomach upset. For suppositories: wash your hands, remove the wrapper, lie on your side with your knees bent, gently push the suppository pointed-end first into your rectum, and stay lying down for a few minutes. Try to hold it in for 15 to 20 minutes before going to the bathroom.
dosing: Adults and children 12 years and older: Tablets — take 1 to 3 tablets (5 mg each) once daily, usually at bedtime so it works by morning. Suppository — use one 10 mg suppository once daily. Children 6 to 11 years: Tablets — 1 tablet once daily. Suppository — half of a 10 mg suppository or as directed by your doctor. Children under 6 years: Ask your doctor before use. Do not use bisacodyl for more than 7 days in a row unless your doctor tells you to.
missed_dose: Bisacodyl is usually taken only when needed, so a regular dosing schedule may not apply. If your doctor has put you on a scheduled dose and you miss it, take it as soon as you remember. However, if it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and continue as normal. Do not take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one.
storage: Store bisacodyl tablets and suppositories at room temperature, between 68°F and 77°F (20°C to 25°C). Keep them away from heat, moisture, and direct sunlight. Do not store suppositories in a warm place — if they get too soft, place them in cool water for a few minutes before use. Keep all medications out of reach of children and pets.
what_to_avoid: Do not take bisacodyl tablets with milk, dairy products, or antacids. Wait at least 1 hour before or after taking these. Avoid using bisacodyl for more than 7 consecutive days without talking to your doctor. Do not use if you have stomach pain, nausea, vomiting, or a sudden change in bowel habits that has lasted more than 2 weeks without seeing your doctor first. Avoid relying on laxatives every day, as this can make your bowels dependent on them to work.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away if you experience: rectal bleeding or blood in your stool, no bowel movement after using bisacodyl for 7 days, severe stomach cramps or pain, nausea or vomiting, signs of dehydration such as feeling very thirsty, dizzy, or urinating less than usual, muscle weakness or irregular heartbeat. These could be signs of a more serious problem that needs medical attention.
when_it_works: Bisacodyl tablets usually work within 6 to 12 hours after taking them. That is why many people take them at bedtime so they have a bowel movement in the morning. Bisacodyl suppositories work faster — usually within 15 to 60 minutes after insertion.
special_populations: Pregnancy: Talk to your doctor before using bisacodyl if you are pregnant. It is generally considered safer to use suppositories than tablets during pregnancy, but always check first. Breastfeeding: Bisacodyl is generally considered safe during breastfeeding, but check with your doctor or pharmacist. Elderly patients: Older adults should use bisacodyl with caution and for the shortest time needed, as overuse can lead to electrolyte imbalances and weakness. Children under 6 years: Do not use without a doctor's guidance. Kidney or liver disease: Talk to your doctor before using bisacodyl if you have kidney or liver problems.
